paras: The attempted lynching of John Gist was a series of efforts by armed white crowds in early August 1888 to take Gist, a Black prisoner, from the Union County jail in Union, South Carolina, and kill him. Sheriff Long and his deputies repulsed a mob of about 75 on the night he was jailed, a militia company was ordered to guard the jail, and a larger armed party was talked out of attacking two nights later. Gist was then moved to Columbia, and the case drew a long commentary from Union on lynchers and the law.

Gist, described as "colored," was accused of criminally assaulting Mrs. Smith Wood, a white woman of Union County, in her husband's absence on Wednesday, August 1. He was lodged in the county jail on Saturday, August 4.

That Saturday night, according to a Union special to the Greenville News, "a mob of 75 strong" tried to lynch him and was repulsed by Sheriff Long and Deputies R. W. Long, T. J. Vinson and L. Moore. The sheriff called on Captain M. W. Culp and the Johnson Rifles, and on Sunday the governor telegraphed Culp to guard the jail while any danger of lynching lasted. By Monday a raid by 200 men was rumored, and a Columbia special reported that men gathering near town had bought five bags of buckshot.

The News and Courier's Union correspondent later wrote, on "good authority," that on Monday night seventy-eight men with Winchester rifles crossed Broad River from Chester County, joined a party on the Union side and halted four miles from town to wait for other crowds. A party of Pinckney men who had watched the town all day met them and, with difficulty, persuaded them to go home, arguing that the rifle company was there on Governor Richardson's order to protect the sheriff rather than the prisoner. On Tuesday, August 7, Sheriff Long took Gist to Columbia and lodged him in the Richland jail for safe keeping.

The Union correspondent reported on August 10 that the town and county "breathed easier" once the sheriff decided to remove the prisoner. No arrests of the would-be lynchers and no report of Gist's trial were found in the coverage.

The episode was covered only by white newspapers, mostly in South Carolina, between August 9 and 16. The Newberry Herald and News reprinted the Greenville News special under "TROUBLE AT UNION. An Attempt at Lynching Defeated," and the Atlanta Constitution ran the Columbia special as "Escaped With the Prisoner"; both stated the assault as fact. The Savannah Morning News, the Yorkville Enquirer and the Baptist Courier gave the threat, the attempt or the removal a sentence each in their state columns.

The longest account, the News and Courier letter reprinted in Newberry as "LYNCHERS AND LYNCHING," took Gist's guilt as settled and called him "the dastardly negro" and "the black scoundrel of a prisoner." Its writer described some of the lynchers as "of the best people of the county" and said most of the riflemen would themselves have liked to hang Gist. He nonetheless urged the state's papers to correct the belief, which he traced to a reported grand-jury charge by Judge Pressly in York County, that "a hundred men constitute the law."
The Baptist Courier dated the attempt on the jail "the 5th," while the specials written from Union and Columbia on August 6 and 7 put it on Saturday night, the day Gist was jailed.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of John Gist
bases: Armed crowds repeatedly tried or prepared to take a prisoner accused of assault from the Union County jail to lynch him and were stopped by the sheriff, a militia company and his removal to Columbia (A1, A3, A5, A6).

No one was killed: the mob of about 75 was repulsed and a later armed party turned back, and Gist was moved to Columbia alive (A1, A2, A5); the episode is an attempted lynching by a group acting on an assault accusation (A3, A6).

Two independent specials, from Union to the Greenville News (A1) and from Columbia (A3), agree on the Saturday attempt and the militia guard, and a third from Union (A5) plus briefs (A2, A4, A6) confirm the threat and the removal.

accounts.label: Union special to the Greenville News
accounts.gist: A mob of 75 tried to lynch Gist on Saturday night and was repulsed by the sheriff and three deputies; the Johnson Rifles were put on guard and a raid by 200 was rumored.

accounts.label: Columbia special
accounts.gist: After the Saturday attempt, a large organized party gathered near town and bought buckshot, and the sheriff brought Gist to Columbia rather than face it.

accounts.label: Union correspondent of the News and Courier
accounts.gist: On 'good authority', 78 armed men from the Chester side and others gathered four miles out on Monday night and were talked into going home by Pinckney men, who told them the rifles were there on the governor's order to protect the sheriff.

framing.detail: Headlined 'TROUBLE AT UNION. An Attempt at Lynching Defeated' and 'Escaped With the Prisoner'; the specials report the attempts without comment but state the assault as fact ('committed an assault').

Under 'LYNCHERS AND LYNCHING ... Vindication of the Law', the Union correspondent took Gist's guilt as certain and used 'a nigger' in the lynchers' words and 'black scoundrel' in his own, praised the lynchers as 'brave and determined', yet urged papers to teach that a crowd is not the law.
Brief state-news items in Savannah, Yorkville and Columbia papers reported only the threat and the removal or the attempt.

conflicts.note: The two Union and Columbia specials written August 6-7 agree on Saturday; the weekly review's date is later and secondhand. The Monday-night approach (A5) is a separate, later gathering.
